screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a clear mental model for how Ethereum charges for computation and why that matters for every dApp user and developer. We start by treating gas as the fuel of the Ethereum Virtual Machine: every operation consumes gas so the network resists spam and validators are compensated. Then we connect that fuel concept to practical knobs you control in a transaction — gasLimit and gasPrice — and show how the total fee is computed. Next, we explain the common denominations you must convert between: Wei, Gwei, and Ether, and why failing to convert correctly causes costly mistakes. Finally, we spend substantial time on EIP-1559: how a dynamically adjusted base fee is burned, how a priority fee functions as a tip to validators, and how maxFee and maxPriorityFee form the new payment guardrails. Throughout, you'll see concrete examples and common beginner mistakes so you can set parameters safely and design gas-efficient contracts. By the end you'll be able to estimate a simple transfer cost and explain the difference between pre- and post-EIP-1559 pricing.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Gas, Gwei, and Transaction Costs
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Gas, Gwei, and Transaction Costs

Understand the measurement of work on Ethereum, how costs are calculated before and after EIP-1559, and practical steps to estimate fees when you build with web3.js.

In this lesson
Gas as fuel and fee mechanics

Why gas prevents abuse and how validators are compensated.

Coming up
EIP-1559 and fee burning

How base fee and priority fee change payment flows.

Practical
Estimating costs with web3.js

A code walkthrough that fetches base fee and computes estimated ETH cost.

Visual summary
Fuel, Price, and Burn
Gas quantifies work. gasLimit sets the cap, EIP-1559's base fee is burned, and priority fee tips validators. Learn to estimate costs and avoid common mistakes like underestimating gasLimit or mis-converting units.
Example
Simple ETH transfer
A standard transfer uses 21,000 gas. If base fee plus tip equals 100 Gwei, multiply gasUsed by that sum and convert from Wei to Ether to find ETH cost.
Why it matters
User experience and cost predictability
Designing gas-efficient contracts reduces user cost and failed transactions, which directly affects your dApp's adoption.
Quick guide
Start by reading the latest base fee on the network, set a sensible maxPriorityFee for speed, and always convert units with web3.utils.toWei/fromWei before computing costs.

screens.title: What is Gas?
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is the accounting unit for every operation executed on Ethereum's virtual machine. At its core, gas measures computational effort: reading and writing storage, performing arithmetic, and executing opcodes each consume a fixed number of gas units. This system has two practical consequences. One, it prevents abuse by attaching a real cost to running code, so endless loops or massive storage writes become prohibitively expensive and cannot spam the network. Two, it compensates the validators for the work of processing blocks. A practical example: a simple Ether transfer consumes 21,000 gas units. If you instead call a function that writes to storage multiple times, gas jumps because storage operations are expensive. A common misconception is to think gas is a vague estimate you can ignore; it is not. If your transaction runs out of gas — you hit gasLimit before completion — the transaction reverts, state changes are undone, but you still pay for the gas consumed. That is why correct estimation matters. Reflect: when you design a contract, which operations will increase gas most — arithmetic or storage — and how will that affect user cost?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Gas quantifies computational work on Ethereum; it prevents denial-of-service attacks and compensates validators.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is Gas?
Definition

Gas is the unit that measures computation cost on the EVM. Each opcode and operation consumes gas, which users pay for to prevent abuse and reward validators.

Concrete example
Simple transfer

A standard ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. More complex contract functions require more gas because they execute many operations.

Common mistake
Underestimating gasLimit

If gasLimit is too low, the transaction reverts but consumed gas is still paid. Always estimate with a buffer for complex calls.

Key Takeaway

Gas is a precise measure of computation. Design and estimate to avoid out-of-gas failures and unexpected user charges.

Analogy

Think of gas like car fuel: each operation consumes a fixed amount of fuel. Running heavy operations is like driving uphill with the air conditioning on — costs more fuel.

Operation cost
Storage writes

Writing to storage is significantly more expensive than arithmetic, so minimize unnecessary writes.

Operation cost
Read and compute

Reads and math are cheaper but still add up inside complex loops.

Question: Which pattern in your contract could you refactor to reduce repeated storage writes and lower gas for users?

screens.title: gasLimit, gasPrice, and transactionFee
screens.narratorSegment: When you create a transaction you are choosing limits and prices that determine whether the transaction runs and how much it costs. Before EIP-1559 the most common model was simple: you set a gasPrice and a gasLimit. GasLimit is the maximum units of gas you permit the transaction to consume. If execution needs more than gasLimit, it runs out of gas, reverts, and you still pay for consumed gas. GasPrice was the wei-per-gas you offered; validators prioritized higher gasPrice transactions because they earned more. The transaction fee in that model is gasUsed times gasPrice. After EIP-1559 the pricing structure changes but the idea of gasLimit remains the same: it protects users from runaway costs. Practically, always select gasLimit conservatively by using an estimate for complex calls and a small safety margin. A concrete example: a token transfer typically consumes 21,000 gas; a complex swap may need 200,000 or more. A frequent misconception is thinking gasLimit is refunded entirely if unused; it is not charged, only gasUsed is charged, but the limit still bounds execution. Closing question: how would you set gasLimit and price for a user-initiated contract call to balance cost and safety?

keyIdea.title: How fees are computed
keyIdea.text: Pre-EIP-1559: transactionFee = gasUsed * gasPrice. Post-EIP-1559: gasLimit still caps consumption but fee components change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › gasLimit, gasPrice, transactionFee
Terminology
  • gasLimit: Maximum gas units a sender permits for the transaction.
  • gasPrice: Wei-per-gas offered (pre-EIP-1559 model).
  • transactionFee: gasUsed multiplied by the per-unit price.
Concrete example
Simple transfer

If gasUsed = 21,000 and gasPrice = 20 Gwei, the total fee is 21,000 times 20 Gwei, converted to Ether.

Visual process
1. Set gasLimit
Choose a cap based on function complexity and an estimate buffer.
2. Price the gas
Pre-EIP-1559 use gasPrice; after EIP-1559 use maxFee and priority fee.
3. Pay for gasUsed
You are charged for the gas actually consumed, up to the gasLimit.
Misconception check: Unused gas within gasLimit is not charged; only gasUsed is paid. However, if the transaction runs out of gas, the transaction reverts but the gas consumed before revert is still lost.

screens.title: Ether Units: Wei, Gwei, Ether
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum represents value in integer units to avoid floating point errors. The smallest unit is Wei: one Ether equals 10 to the 18th Wei. For gas pricing, Gwei is the common human-friendly unit: one Gwei equals 1,000,000,000 Wei or 10 to the 9th Wei. When gas prices are quoted as, for example, 20 Gwei, they mean 20 billion Wei per gas unit. This arithmetic matters because multiplying gas units by a per-unit price quickly generates very large Wei values, and you must convert back to Ether to display a sensible user-facing number. Web3. js provides web3. utils. toWei and fromWei to handle conversions reliably. A common beginner error is multiplying a gas value in Gwei by gasUsed while forgetting to convert to Wei, causing the displayed Ether cost to be off by orders of magnitude. Concrete example: if gasUsed = 21,000 and price = 20 Gwei, compute total Wei as BigInt(gasUsed) * BigInt(priceInWei) then convert that Wei to Ether with fromWei for display. Misconception check: never assume the unit; always convert explicitly. How will you ensure every UI string that mentions prices has been converted and formatted safely?

keyIdea.text: Use Wei for internal arithmetic, Gwei for human gas-price entry, and Ether for end-user display; always convert explicitly with web3.utils.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Ether Units
Unit table
  • Wei: smallest unit, 1 Ether = 10^18 Wei.
  • Gwei: 1 Gwei = 10^9 Wei, common for gas prices.
  • Ether: user-facing currency, convert for display.
Example calculation
Convert and compute

Multiply gasUsed by priceInWei, then convert the resulting Wei to Ether for display with web3.utils.fromWei.

Quick code pattern
// Example pattern (pseudocode)
const gasUsed = 21000n;
const priceGwei = '20';
const priceWei = web3.utils.toWei(priceGwei, 'gwei');
const totalWei = gasUsed * BigInt(priceWei);
const totalEth = web3.utils.fromWei(totalWei.toString(), 'ether');
// display totalEth to user
Misconception: Treating Gwei or Ether as interchangeable without explicit conversion will break cost displays. Always use toWei/fromWei for arithmetic and UI formatting.

screens.title: Pre-EIP-1559: First-Price Auction
screens.narratorSegment: Before EIP-1559, Ethereum used a first-price auction model for fees: users specified a gasPrice and miners picked the highest-paying transactions to include. This model made fees volatile because users frequently overbid to secure inclusion quickly, and simple heuristics often led to overpayment. The concrete effect was unpredictable UX: one block users paid a few Gwei, the next block spikes made identical transactions cost much more. Developers had to implement gas oracles and user prompts to estimate safe gasPrice. A practical example of the problem: during congestion, wallets recommended increasingly higher gasPrice values and users could inadvertently pay far more than necessary. Misconception: some assume the network simply queues transactions until gasPrice drops; in reality, low-priced transactions can sit pending indefinitely or be dropped. The auction also lacked a deflationary mechanism because all fees went to miners. Understanding this history explains why EIP-1559 was designed to improve predictability and introduce base fee burning. Ask yourself: how did unpredictable fees affect your users' trust in a dApp using the old model? Pre-EIP-1559: First-Price Auction means pre-eip-1559 fees were a simple auction; this led to volatility and overpaying without predictable base prices.. In practical terms, how transactions were prioritized and why fees were volatile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Pre-EIP-1559 Auction
How it worked

Users bid a gasPrice. Miners prioritized highest bids. Fees were paid entirely to miners, and congestion led to bidding wars.

Example
Spike during congestion

When blocks filled, wallets recommended higher gasPrice, causing many users to overpay to get inclusion fast.

Downside
Unpredictability

Users couldn't reliably predict what price would be necessary for timely inclusion, harming UX.

Developer impact
  • Need for gas oracles and complex wallet logic.
  • Refunds or retries when transactions underpriced or pending indefinitely.
  • Difficulty explaining fees to users in a predictable way.
Reflective question: If your dApp relied on fast inclusion for UX, how did you protect users from paying excessive gasPrice in the auction model?

screens.title: EIP-1559: Base Fee and Priority Fee
screens.narratorSegment: EIP-1559 restructured how transaction fees are calculated to make costs more predictable and to create a burning mechanism for part of the fee. The two central components are the base fee and the priority fee. The base fee is a network-determined amount that adjusts block-by-block: if a block is more than 50% full, the base fee increases; if less than 50% full, it decreases. Importantly, the base fee is burned, removing that Ether from circulation rather than paying validators. The priority fee — sometimes called a tip — is an optional amount the user pays directly to the validator to incentivize faster inclusion. Practically, when you submit a transaction under EIP-1559 you provide a maxFeePerGas and a maxPriorityFeePerGas. The actual amount charged per gas unit is baseFee plus the actualPriorityFee; any leftover from maxFeePerGas beyond what is used is refunded to the sender. A frequent misconception is thinking the base fee goes to the validator; it does not. Consider how burning base fee can affect the token economics and how providing a competitive priority fee can speed inclusion during congestion.

keyIdea.title: EIP-1559 essentials
keyIdea.text: Base fee is burned and dynamically adjusted; priority fee goes to validators to prioritize transactions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › EIP-1559 Components
Base fee

Network-set fee that adjusts with congestion and is burned. It stabilizes pricing by responding to block fullness.

Priority fee (tip)

Optional tip to validators that speeds inclusion. Unlike the base fee, this amount goes directly to the validator.

Misconception
Base fee is not a tip

People sometimes assume the base fee rewards validators; in reality it is burned, changing economic incentives.

Payment flow
  • maxFeePerGas: The most you're willing to pay per gas unit.
  • maxPriorityFeePerGas: Your tip ceiling to the validator.
  • actualPriorityFee: The lesser of maxPriorityFeePerGas and maxFeePerGas minus baseFee.
Key Takeaway

EIP-1559 makes fees more predictable and burns base fee; use maxFee and maxPriorityFee to protect users from sudden spikes.

screens.title: How maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas Work
screens.narratorSegment: Under EIP-1559 you submit two upper bounds and the network computes what you actually pay. maxFeePerGas is the absolute maximum you're willing to pay per gas unit, covering both base fee and priority fee. maxPriorityFeePerGas is the maximum tip you offer validators. When the transaction is processed, the actual per-unit cost is baseFee plus actualPriorityFee. The actualPriorityFee equals the smaller of your maxPriorityFeePerGas and the remaining margin available (maxFeePerGas minus baseFee). Any portion of maxFeePerGas that exceeds baseFee plus actualPriorityFee is refunded to the sender. An example helps: suppose baseFee is 50 Gwei, maxPriorityFeePerGas is 3 Gwei, and maxFeePerGas is 60 Gwei. The actualPriorityFee will be min(3, 60-50) = min(3,10) = 3 Gwei, so the per-unit cost is 53 Gwei. If you set maxFeePerGas much higher than necessary you will be refunded the difference, but setting maxFeePerGas too low can prevent inclusion if baseFee rises. Misconception: refunds do not eliminate the need to choose sensible bounds; you should pick realistic maxFee and priority fee to balance safety and speed. How would you choose values for a user-facing default? How maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas Work means actualfeepergas = basefee + actualpriorityfee; actualpriorityfee = min(maxpriorityfeepergas, maxfeepergas - basefee).. In practical terms, calculation, refunds, and the actual priority fee. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Payment formula
keyIdea.text: actualFeePerGas = baseFee + actualPriorityFee; actualPriorityFee = min(maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas - baseFee).

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › maxFee & maxPriorityFee
Three-step calculation
  1. Network sets baseFee for the block.
  2. actualPriorityFee = min(maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas - baseFee).
  3. Actual per-unit cost = baseFee + actualPriorityFee; refund any unused portion of maxFeePerGas.
Concrete example
Numbers in Gwei

If baseFee=50, maxPriorityFee=3, maxFee=60, actual per-unit = 50 + 3 = 53 Gwei; remainder refunded.

Practical advice
  • Pick maxFeePerGas slightly above expected baseFee to allow headroom for fluctuations.
  • Choose maxPriorityFeePerGas to reflect how urgently you need inclusion.
  • Rely on oracles or real-time estimates to set defaults in a wallet UI.
Misconception check: A large maxFeePerGas does not mean validators get more—they only receive the tip; the base fee is burned.

screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through a hands-on example: using web3. js to read the latest block base fee and estimate the cost of a simple Ether transfer. The provided script connects to a provider, fetches the latest block to discover baseFeePerGas, and computes total cost for a transfer using a suggested priority fee range. Key points: baseFeePerGas in the block is expressed in Wei, so convert it to Gwei for human readability and to Wei for arithmetic. The example multiplies a simple transfer gasLimit of 21,000 by the sum of base fee and a recommended priority fee to estimate totalWei, then converts that to ETH for display. A common mistake is to trust web3. eth. getGasPrice alone for EIP-1559 pricing — it's a blended estimate and lacks the explicit base/prio split. When you run this script, you should inspect the numerical outputs and reflect on how baseFeePerGas changes between runs; this demonstrates the dynamic nature of EIP-1559 fees. Misconception: the recommended priority fee values are only a guide — for urgent inclusion you may need to increase the tip. How would you surface these numbers to users without causing confusion?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Estimating with web3.js
What the script does
  • Fetch the latest block to read baseFeePerGas (in Wei).
  • Define recommended low and high priority fees in Gwei and convert to Wei.
  • Compute maxFeePerGas as baseFee plus priority fee and multiply by gasLimit to estimate total cost.
Developer tip
Always convert units

Use web3.utils.toWei/fromWei. Store and compute in Wei to avoid precision issues, then format Ether for the user.

Code (estimateGas.js)
const Web3 = require('web3');

const INFURA_PROJECT_ID = 'YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID'; 
const providerUrl = `https://mainnet.infura.io/v3/${INFURA_PROJECT_ID}`;
const web3 = new Web3(providerUrl);

async function getGasEstimates() {
  try {
    console.log('Fetching EIP-1559 gas price estimates...');

    // Get the latest block to find the base fee
    const latestBlock = await web3.eth.getBlock('latest');
    const baseFeePerGas = BigInt(latestBlock.baseFeePerGas);

    // Let's simulate a recommended priority fee range (in Wei)
    const recommendedLowPriorityFee = web3.utils.toWei('1', 'gwei'); // 1 Gwei
    const recommendedHighPriorityFee = web3.utils.toWei('3', 'gwei'); // 3 Gwei

    // Example: Calculate cost for a simple Ether transfer (21,000 gas limit)
    const gasLimitSimpleTransfer = 21000;

    const maxFeePerGasLow = baseFeePerGas + BigInt(recommendedLowPriorityFee);
    const totalCostLow = BigInt(gasLimitSimpleTransfer) * maxFeePerGasLow;

    console.log(`Base Fee Per Gas: ${web3.utils.fromWei(baseFeePerGas.toString(), 'gwei')} Gwei`);
    console.log(`Total Estimated Cost (low tip): ${web3.utils.fromWei(totalCostLow.toString(), 'ether')} ETH`);

  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error fetching gas estimates:', error);
  }
}

getGasEstimates();
Reminder: replace YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID and run node estimateGas.js. Observe how baseFeePerGas varies across runs and how recommended priority fees affect the estimate.

screens.title: Designing Gas-Efficient Smart Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Gas cost is not only a runtime detail; it shapes the design of your contracts and the user experience of your dApp. The strongest gas savings come from reducing expensive operations such as storage writes and using efficient data structures. For example, prefer mappings over arrays for lookups when you need constant-time access instead of iterating and paying per-item gas. Batch operations can sometimes save gas by amortizing fixed costs across many items, but be mindful of block gas limits. Another strategy is to shift off-chain work for expensive computations and only store necessary results on-chain, which reduces repeated gas payments. Provide clear estimates and fallback behavior in your UI: if a call may require more than a typical gasLimit, warn users and show possible cost ranges. A common misconception is thinking compiler optimizations alone will solve gas problems; while helpful, algorithmic choices matter more. Concrete example: updating a counter in storage each time costs more than computing ephemeral values in memory; restructure logic to minimize persistent state writes. Closing thought: when you optimize for gas you improve adoption because your users pay less and experience fewer failed transactions.

Patterns to reduce gas
  • Minimize storage writes: Storage is expensive; cache or batch writes.
  • Choose efficient structures: Mappings for lookup, avoid unbounded loops.
  • Move heavy work off-chain: Compute off-chain and verify on-chain where possible.
Concrete scenario
Batch token processing

Process multiple items in a single transaction to amortize fixed gas overhead, but watch block gas limits to avoid failures.

UX guidance

Show estimated gas and cost ranges, offer a safety toggle for higher gas limits, and explain why a transaction might fail with out-of-gas rather than blaming the network.

Pro tip

Instrument contract functions with view-only estimation calls so the UI can present realistic gas and refund expectations before users sign.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When working with gas and fees, several recurring mistakes trip up developers and users. The most common is underestimating gasLimit for complex interactions; when a transaction runs out of gas it reverts but you still pay for consumed gas, which leads to frustrated users. Another frequent error is unit confusion: treating Gwei as Wei or forgetting to convert before arithmetic causes displayed costs to be off by large factors. A third pitfall is setting very high maxPriorityFeePerGas or maxFeePerGas without explaining refunds, which can alarm users if they see large numbers temporarily reserved in their wallet. Troubleshooting starts by reading the transaction receipt for gasUsed, checking block baseFeePerGas, and verifying unit conversions with web3. utils. toWei/fromWei. Use view-only estimateGas calls to detect likely failure and present a recommended gasLimit. When a transaction fails with out-of-gas, explain that state changes were undone but consumed gas is still paid. Closing question: which of these errors have you seen in logs or user reports, and how would you instrument your dApp to catch them earlier? If gasLimit is too low, the transaction reverts and consumed gas is not refunded. Use estimateGas and add a margin for complexity.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s summarize the essential concepts to keep front of mind. First, gas is the unit of computation on Ethereum; it prevents abuse and compensates validators. Keep these points in mind when estimating costs, designing contracts, and building wallet UI so users avoid surprise charges and failed transactions. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a clear mental model for how Ethereum charges for computation and why that matters for every dApp user and developer. We start by treating gas as the fuel of the Ethereum Virtual Machine: every operation consumes gas so the network resists spam and validators are compensated. Then we connect that fuel concept to practical knobs you control in a transaction — gasLimit and gasPrice — and show how the total fee is computed. Next, we explain the common denominations you must convert between: Wei, Gwei, and Ether, and why failing to convert correctly causes costly mistakes. Finally, we spend substantial time on EIP-1559: how a dynamically adjusted base fee is burned, how a priority fee functions as a tip to validators, and how maxFee and maxPriorityFee form the new payment guardrails. Throughout, you'll see concrete examples and common beginner mistakes so you can set parameters safely and design gas-efficient contracts. By the end you'll be able to estimate a simple transfer cost and explain the difference between pre- and post-EIP-1559 pricing.

In this screen we make explicit the skills you'll gain so you can track progress. First, you will be able to define gas in Ethereum and explain how it prevents abuse while compensating validators. Knowing that definition helps you reason about why gas is required for every operation. Second, you'll learn to distinguish gasLimit, gasPrice, and transactionFee and how each contributes to the total cost. This skill prevents common mistakes like underestimating a contract call's gasLimit. Third, you will gain fluency with units: Wei, Gwei, and Ether, and how to convert safely using web3. js utilities. Incorrect unit conversion is a frequent source of bugs and wrong-cost displays. Fourth, you'll understand EIP-1559: base fee, priority fee, and how burning changes the economics of Ether. Recognizing these components lets you set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas without overpaying and helps you design clearer user prompts about expected costs.

Take a moment to connect each objective to a concrete developer task. Defining gas matters when you estimate costs for a contract call or design loops and storage patterns. Differentiating gasLimit and gasPrice matters when you prepare transactions for users — if gasLimit is too low a transaction reverts but still consumes gas. Fluency with Wei and Gwei matters whenever you display prices, compute refunds, or read values from the chain; a wrong conversion yields misleading balances. Finally, understanding EIP-1559's base fee and priority fee matters for UX: the base fee is burned so users pay less to validators, but they still need a priority fee to speed inclusion during congestion. Each skill directly reduces failed transactions, incorrect cost displays, and surprised users, which improves trust in your dApp. Learning Objectives (Review) means these four skills reduce failed transactions and wrong-cost displays, improving user trust and dapp reliability.. In practical terms, how these skills appear in practice and why they matter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Gas is the accounting unit for every operation executed on Ethereum's virtual machine. At its core, gas measures computational effort: reading and writing storage, performing arithmetic, and executing opcodes each consume a fixed number of gas units. This system has two practical consequences. One, it prevents abuse by attaching a real cost to running code, so endless loops or massive storage writes become prohibitively expensive and cannot spam the network. Two, it compensates the validators for the work of processing blocks. A practical example: a simple Ether transfer consumes 21,000 gas units. If you instead call a function that writes to storage multiple times, gas jumps because storage operations are expensive. A common misconception is to think gas is a vague estimate you can ignore; it is not. If your transaction runs out of gas — you hit gasLimit before completion — the transaction reverts, state changes are undone, but you still pay for the gas consumed. That is why correct estimation matters. Reflect: when you design a contract, which operations will increase gas most — arithmetic or storage — and how will that affect user cost?

When you create a transaction you are choosing limits and prices that determine whether the transaction runs and how much it costs. Before EIP-1559 the most common model was simple: you set a gasPrice and a gasLimit. GasLimit is the maximum units of gas you permit the transaction to consume. If execution needs more than gasLimit, it runs out of gas, reverts, and you still pay for consumed gas. GasPrice was the wei-per-gas you offered; validators prioritized higher gasPrice transactions because they earned more. The transaction fee in that model is gasUsed times gasPrice. After EIP-1559 the pricing structure changes but the idea of gasLimit remains the same: it protects users from runaway costs. Practically, always select gasLimit conservatively by using an estimate for complex calls and a small safety margin. A concrete example: a token transfer typically consumes 21,000 gas; a complex swap may need 200,000 or more. A frequent misconception is thinking gasLimit is refunded entirely if unused; it is not charged, only gasUsed is charged, but the limit still bounds execution. Closing question: how would you set gasLimit and price for a user-initiated contract call to balance cost and safety?

Ethereum represents value in integer units to avoid floating point errors. The smallest unit is Wei: one Ether equals 10 to the 18th Wei. For gas pricing, Gwei is the common human-friendly unit: one Gwei equals 1,000,000,000 Wei or 10 to the 9th Wei. When gas prices are quoted as, for example, 20 Gwei, they mean 20 billion Wei per gas unit. This arithmetic matters because multiplying gas units by a per-unit price quickly generates very large Wei values, and you must convert back to Ether to display a sensible user-facing number. Web3. js provides web3. utils. toWei and fromWei to handle conversions reliably. A common beginner error is multiplying a gas value in Gwei by gasUsed while forgetting to convert to Wei, causing the displayed Ether cost to be off by orders of magnitude. Concrete example: if gasUsed = 21,000 and price = 20 Gwei, compute total Wei as BigInt(gasUsed) * BigInt(priceInWei) then convert that Wei to Ether with fromWei for display. Misconception check: never assume the unit; always convert explicitly. How will you ensure every UI string that mentions prices has been converted and formatted safely?

Before EIP-1559, Ethereum used a first-price auction model for fees: users specified a gasPrice and miners picked the highest-paying transactions to include. This model made fees volatile because users frequently overbid to secure inclusion quickly, and simple heuristics often led to overpayment. The concrete effect was unpredictable UX: one block users paid a few Gwei, the next block spikes made identical transactions cost much more. Developers had to implement gas oracles and user prompts to estimate safe gasPrice. A practical example of the problem: during congestion, wallets recommended increasingly higher gasPrice values and users could inadvertently pay far more than necessary. Misconception: some assume the network simply queues transactions until gasPrice drops; in reality, low-priced transactions can sit pending indefinitely or be dropped. The auction also lacked a deflationary mechanism because all fees went to miners. Understanding this history explains why EIP-1559 was designed to improve predictability and introduce base fee burning. Ask yourself: how did unpredictable fees affect your users' trust in a dApp using the old model? Pre-EIP-1559: First-Price Auction means pre-eip-1559 fees were a simple auction; this led to volatility and overpaying without predictable base prices.. In practical terms, how transactions were prioritized and why fees were volatile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EIP-1559 restructured how transaction fees are calculated to make costs more predictable and to create a burning mechanism for part of the fee. The two central components are the base fee and the priority fee. The base fee is a network-determined amount that adjusts block-by-block: if a block is more than 50% full, the base fee increases; if less than 50% full, it decreases. Importantly, the base fee is burned, removing that Ether from circulation rather than paying validators. The priority fee — sometimes called a tip — is an optional amount the user pays directly to the validator to incentivize faster inclusion. Practically, when you submit a transaction under EIP-1559 you provide a maxFeePerGas and a maxPriorityFeePerGas. The actual amount charged per gas unit is baseFee plus the actualPriorityFee; any leftover from maxFeePerGas beyond what is used is refunded to the sender. A frequent misconception is thinking the base fee goes to the validator; it does not. Consider how burning base fee can affect the token economics and how providing a competitive priority fee can speed inclusion during congestion.

Under EIP-1559 you submit two upper bounds and the network computes what you actually pay. maxFeePerGas is the absolute maximum you're willing to pay per gas unit, covering both base fee and priority fee. maxPriorityFeePerGas is the maximum tip you offer validators. When the transaction is processed, the actual per-unit cost is baseFee plus actualPriorityFee. The actualPriorityFee equals the smaller of your maxPriorityFeePerGas and the remaining margin available (maxFeePerGas minus baseFee). Any portion of maxFeePerGas that exceeds baseFee plus actualPriorityFee is refunded to the sender. An example helps: suppose baseFee is 50 Gwei, maxPriorityFeePerGas is 3 Gwei, and maxFeePerGas is 60 Gwei. Gas cost is not only a runtime detail; it shapes the design of your contracts and the user experience of your dApp. The strongest gas savings come from reducing expensive operations such as storage writes and using efficient data structures. For example, prefer mappings over arrays for lookups when you need constant-time access instead of iterating and paying per-item gas. Batch operations can sometimes save gas by amortizing fixed costs across many items, but be mindful of block gas limits. Another strategy is to shift off-chain work for expensive computations and only store necessary results on-chain, which reduces repeated gas payments. Provide clear estimates and fallback behavior in your UI: if a call may require more than a typical gasLimit, warn users and show possible cost ranges. A common misconception is thinking compiler optimizations alone will solve gas problems; while helpful, algorithmic choices matter more. Concrete example: updating a counter in storage each time costs more than computing ephemeral values in memory; restructure logic to minimize persistent state writes. Closing thought: when you optimize for gas you improve adoption because your users pay less and experience fewer failed transactions.

Another frequent error is unit confusion: treating Gwei as Wei or forgetting to convert before arithmetic causes displayed costs to be off by large factors. A third pitfall is setting very high maxPriorityFeePerGas or maxFeePerGas without explaining refunds, which can alarm users if they see large numbers temporarily reserved in their wallet. Let’s summarize the essential concepts to keep front of mind. First, gas is the unit of computation on Ethereum; it prevents abuse and compensates validators. Second, gasLimit is a cap on execution while gasPrice or EIP-1559 parameters determine the per-unit payment; if you run out of gas the transaction reverts but consumed gas is paid. Third, use Wei for arithmetic, Gwei for gas pricing inputs, and Ether for user displays; always convert explicitly. Fourth, EIP-1559 introduced a base fee that the network burns and a priority fee that goes to validators; users now set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas which result in refunds if over-provisioned. Keep these points in mind when estimating costs, designing contracts, and building wallet UI so users avoid surprise charges and failed transactions.
